findings.claim: The Table timeline stops in 1559, so it omits the formation of the two largest believer's-baptism families in America and, in particular, the one position the axis cannot describe (believer's immersion for remission with a weekly Supper).
findings.evidence: Entries: 110, 1215, 1525, 1529, 1559. Nothing on the English Baptists (1609/1644) or the Stone-Campbell movement.
findings.fix: Add after Calvin: '1843 Campbell-Rice debate, Lexington: the Stone-Campbell movement argues believer's immersion "for the remission of sins" (Acts 2:38) with a weekly Supper, sacramental in effect, memorial in the Supper.'

findings.lens: Presbyterian / Reformed (Westminster Standards, Three Forms of Unity)
findings.claim: Dating the Reformed spiritual presence to 'Calvin's final Institutes' (1559) makes it look like one man's late opinion; the Reformed churches united on it in 1549 and confessed it in 1561-63.
findings.evidence: Consensus Tigurinus (1549), Calvin and Bullinger: Christ truly given in the Supper by the Spirit to faith; Belgic Confession 35 (1561); Heidelberg Catechism 75-79 (1563); WCF 29.7 (1646).
findings.fix: { "when": "1549", "what": "Consensus Tigurinus: Calvin and Bullinger unite the Reformed churches on a real presence given by the Spirit and received by faith; confessed in Belgic 35 and Heidelberg 75–79." }

findings.claim: The only Baptist marker on the Table timeline is '1525 First believer's baptisms in Zurich; the Anabaptist movement begins', which implies English Particular Baptists descend from the Anabaptists. They arose from Puritan separatism and said so, and their confession puts a Calvinist Supper inside a credobaptist body, which is the whole point this axis mis-scores.
findings.evidence: First London Confession (1644) title page: 'commonly (though falsely) called Anabaptists'; 1689 LBC 29.4 (immersion) with 30.7 (spiritual presence).
findings.fix: Add a sixth entry after 1559: {when: '1644 / 1689', what: 'The Particular Baptists\' London Confessions: believer\'s baptism by immersion, with Christ "spiritually present to the faith of believers" at the Supper.'}
